stem: A wildlife sanctuary houses 83 reptiles. Of these, 29 are turtles, 37 are lizards, and 17 are snakes. If one reptile is selected at random, what is the probability that it is a lizard?
explanation: The probability of selecting a lizard is the number of lizards divided by the total number of reptiles: $\frac{37}{83}$. The value $\frac{29}{83}$ results from selecting the turtle count instead. The value $\frac{17}{83}$ results from selecting the snake count instead. The value $\frac{37}{54}$ results from dividing by the number of non-turtle reptiles ($83 - 29 = 54$) instead of the total, using a subset as the denominator.

stem: At a ceramics studio, 143 pieces were fired in a kiln last month. Of the 61 bowls, 14 cracked during firing. Of the 82 vases, 23 cracked during firing. If a piece is selected at random from those that cracked, what is the probability that it is a vase?
explanation: The total number of cracked pieces is $14 + 23 = 37$. The probability that a randomly selected cracked piece is a vase is $\frac{23}{37}$. The value $\frac{23}{82}$ incorrectly uses the total vase count as the denominator, finding the probability a vase cracked rather than conditioning on being cracked. The value $\frac{23}{143}$ uses the overall total as the denominator, ignoring the condition. The value $\frac{14}{37}$ gives the probability a cracked piece is a bowl, not a vase.

stem: A shipping warehouse inspects packages on two conveyor lines. Line P processes 270 packages per day and Line Q processes 180 packages per day. On Line P, 3% of packages are flagged as damaged. On Line Q, 7% of packages are flagged as damaged. A package is selected at random from all packages processed that day. Given that the package was flagged as damaged, what is the probability that it came from Line Q, to the nearest thousandth?
explanation: Line P flags $0.03 \times 270 = 8.1$ packages on average, and Line Q flags $0.07 \times 180 = 12.6$ packages. The total flagged is $8.1 + 12.6 = 20.7$. By Bayes' theorem, the probability a flagged package came from Line Q is $\frac{12.6}{20.7} \approx 0.609$. The value $0.400$ comes from using the ratio of line volumes $\frac{180}{450}$ without accounting for different damage rates. The value $0.070$ is simply the damage rate on Line Q, ignoring the conditioning. The value $0.500$ assumes equal likelihood from each line, disregarding both volume and rate differences.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 400 subscribers to an online magazine found that 58% preferred reading articles on mobile devices. The margin of error for this estimate is 4.9 percentage points at the 95% confidence level. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly 58% of all subscribers prefer reading on mobile devices.
It is plausible that between 53.1% and 62.9% of all subscribers prefer reading on mobile devices.
Between 53.1% and 62.9% of the 400 sampled subscribers prefer reading on mobile devices.
If another sample of 400 subscribers is taken, exactly 58% will prefer reading on mobile devices.

explanation: The margin of error creates a confidence interval of $58\% \pm 4.9\%$, or $53.1\%$ to $62.9\%$, for the population parameter. This means it is plausible that the true proportion of all subscribers who prefer mobile falls within this range. Stating that exactly 58% of all subscribers prefer mobile treats the sample statistic as the exact population value. Applying the interval to the sample rather than the population confuses who the inference is about. Claiming a new sample will yield exactly 58% misunderstands sampling variability.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A botanist surveys a random sample of 625 trees in a national forest and finds that 41% show signs of bark beetle damage. The margin of error is 3.9 percentage points at the 95% confidence level. The forest contains 28,750 trees total. Which of the following is the best estimate of the number of trees in the entire forest showing signs of bark beetle damage?

options.text: Between 10,661 and 12,904
Between 256 and 281
Between 10,063 and 12,938
Exactly 11,788

explanation: The confidence interval for the proportion is $41\% \pm 3.9\%$, or $37.1\%$ to $44.9\%$. Applying this to the population of 28,750 trees: $0.371 \times 28{,}750 = 10{,}661.25$ and $0.449 \times 28{,}750 = 12{,}903.75$, giving approximately 10,661 to 12,904 trees. The range 256 to 281 applies the percentages to the sample size of 625 instead of the population. The range 10,063 to 12,938 results from rounding errors in the percentage calculation ($35\%$ to $45\%$ instead of $37.1\%$ to $44.9\%$). Exactly 11,788 treats the point estimate ($0.41 \times 28{,}750$) as exact, ignoring the margin of error entirely.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Two independent random samples are drawn from the same city's registered voters. Sample A (n = 500) finds 47% support a transit proposal with a margin of error of 4.5 percentage points. Sample B (n = 1,250) finds 53% support the same proposal with a margin of error of 2.8 percentage points. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.text: The two samples contradict each other, so neither result is reliable.
Sample B is more reliable because it has a larger sample size, so the true support is exactly 53%.
Because the confidence intervals from the two samples overlap, it is plausible that the true level of support falls within both intervals.
The true proportion must be exactly halfway between the two estimates, at 50%.

explanation: Sample A's confidence interval is $42.5\%$ to $51.5\%$, and Sample B's is $50.2\%$ to $55.8\%$. These intervals overlap in the range $50.2\%$ to $51.5\%$, so it is plausible the true proportion lies in both intervals simultaneously. Claiming the samples contradict each other ignores the overlap region. Stating the true value is exactly 53% conflates a larger sample with perfect precision and ignores the margin of error. Averaging the two point estimates to get 50% has no statistical basis and ignores the different precisions of the two estimates.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A school district compared standardized test scores of students who voluntarily enrolled in an after-school tutoring program with scores of students who did not enroll. The district found that students in the tutoring program scored higher on average. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The tutoring program caused the higher test scores.
There is an association between enrolling in the tutoring program and higher test scores.
Students who did not enroll would have scored higher if they had enrolled.
The tutoring program is equally effective for all students in the district.

explanation: Because students voluntarily enrolled, this is an observational study, not an experiment with random assignment. Observational studies can identify associations but cannot establish causation. Confounding variables (such as motivation or prior achievement) may explain the difference. Claiming the program caused the higher scores requires a randomized experiment. Stating that non-enrolled students would have scored higher if enrolled assumes a causal effect not supported by the design. Claiming equal effectiveness for all students goes beyond what any single comparison can show.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers wanted to test whether a new ergonomic keyboard reduces wrist strain. They recruited 174 office workers and allowed each participant to choose whether to use the new keyboard or keep their standard keyboard for 8 weeks. At the end of the study, the group using the new keyboard reported 31% less wrist strain on average. Which of the following is the most significant flaw in the study design?

options.text: The study lasted only 8 weeks, which may not be long enough.
Participants were not randomly assigned to the keyboard groups, so confounding variables may explain the difference.
The sample size of 174 is too small to detect any difference.
The study should have included a third group using a different ergonomic keyboard.

explanation: The critical flaw is that participants self-selected into groups rather than being randomly assigned. Workers who chose the ergonomic keyboard may differ systematically from those who kept their standard keyboard (e.g., in ergonomic awareness, typing habits, or preexisting wrist conditions), creating confounding variables that could explain the observed difference. While study duration is a practical consideration, it is not the primary design flaw. A sample of 174 is not inherently too small for a two-group comparison. Adding a third keyboard group would not address the fundamental issue of self-selection bias.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A pharmaceutical company conducted a randomized controlled trial with 1,380 participants to test a new anti-inflammatory cream. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either the active cream or an identical-looking placebo cream applied twice daily for 12 weeks. Neither the participants nor the physicians measuring outcomes knew which cream each participant received. At the end of the trial, the group using the active cream showed a statistically significant reduction in inflammation compared to the placebo group. However, the company then marketed the cream to teenagers, a demographic that was not included in the trial (all participants were ages 35 to 70). Which of the following best describes the limitation of applying the trial's results to teenagers?

options.text: The trial did not use random assignment, so causation cannot be established.
The trial was not double-blind, so the placebo effect may account for the results.
The results may not generalize to teenagers because the sample did not include that age group.
The 12-week duration was too short for any meaningful conclusion about the cream's effectiveness.

explanation: The trial was well-designed: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, and yielded statistically significant results within its studied population (ages 35 to 70). The limitation is one of generalizability: since no teenagers were included, the results cannot be directly extended to that age group, whose physiology and inflammatory responses may differ. Claiming the trial lacked random assignment contradicts the stated design. Claiming it was not double-blind contradicts the description that neither participants nor physicians knew which cream was administered. While study duration is always a consideration, the question specifically asks about the limitation of applying results to teenagers, which is a generalizability issue.
